sections.rawHeading: 1 · Licensing (GOV — high confidence; a real statewide license that reaches masonry)
sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence; a real statewide license that reaches masonry
sections.markdown: **West Virginia is a genuine statewide-license state — and its license reaches chimney repair work at $5,000+ residential.** STATE LAW: the **West Virginia Contractor Licensing Act — RECODIFIED at W. Va. Code ch. 30, art. 42 (§§ 30-42-1 to -20); former § 21-11 is repealed (§§ 21-11-3, -6, -7, -8 all "[Repealed]" verified on code.wvlegislature.gov Jul 10, 2026)** — run by the **WV Contractor Licensing Board (Division of Labor)**, requires a contractor license for work with total cost of **$5,000 or more residential / $25,000 commercial (§ 30-42-3(d), fetched)** — raised from the earlier $2,500. The statute's definitions (§ 30-42-3) name classifications — electrical, general building, general engineering, HVAC, piping, plumbing, residential, and **specialty** contractors — but **do not name a masonry classification; any "Masonry" specialty (and its tuckpointing scope) lives in Board rules that were NOT read in Sep 2026 — UNVERIFIED, do not publish the masonry-class detail.** Chimney rebuild, reline, and repointing at $5,000+ (residential) require an **active WV contractor license** in an appropriate classification. Exemptions (§ 30-42-6) include owner-occupant work and material suppliers; § 30-42-20 makes state licensing exclusive of local licensing. Public lookup: **labor.wv.gov** Contractor Licensing Board / license search. This is stronger than much of the mid-Atlantic norm.

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: Narrower than in no-license states but still real: the WV licensing exams test **contracting/business and trade knowledge** *(exam content not re-read Sep 2026)*, not flue diagnosis or NFPA 211 compliance. A licensed contractor can rebuild a chimney to code without ever being trained to inspect one. Also note the **SWEEP vs REPAIR split**: routine **chimney sweeping/cleaning** falls **below the $5,000 residential threshold** (now even more comfortably, after the raise), so a sweep-only operator lawfully needs **no** state contractor license — while a large *repair* that follows does. The raised floor also un-licenses more of the mid-size repair market (a $3,500 repoint no longer requires the license). Licensing-research batch 2 adds a second hole: **the HVAC technician certification (§ 21-16) expressly excludes decorative fireplaces/stoves not used as primary heat (§ 21-16-2(b)(1))** *(Jul 2026 batch-2 cite; not re-read Sep 2026)* — a gas-log service call on a decorative unit under $5,000 may lawfully need nothing. Individual certs (CSIA CCS, C-DET; NCSG CCP/CCR) remain the competence signal for the inspection itself.

sections.rawHeading: 3 · Home sale (GOV absence check on code article lists — no disclosure statute located; statute name/section UNVERIFIED)
sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.confidenceNote: absence check on code article lists — no disclosure statute located; statute name/section UNVERIFIED
sections.markdown: STATE LAW: West Virginia is a **caveat emptor** state with **no statutory seller-disclosure article found in the current Code**. The prior draft cited a "West Virginia Residential Property Condition Disclosure Act" in Chapter 36; **the current Chapter 36 (Estates and Property, Arts. 1–13) and Chapter 37 (Real Property, Arts. 1–15) article lists on code.wvlegislature.gov contain no disclosure act** (checked Sep 15, 2026). Its existence and any codified section are **UNVERIFIED — do not publish that Act name or any section number.** Absence as finding (pending a full-code search): no mandatory state disclosure form was located. A Realtor-association **seller's disclosure statement** is reportedly the form in market use, with an "as is" option *(REF, not re-verified; the earlier "buyer can waive in writing" claim depended on the unverified Act and is withdrawn)*. So the chimney is disclosed only if the seller volunteers it. Fraud/active concealment remains actionable at common law. No inspection is mandated at transfer; NFPA 211 Level 2 stays a NATIONAL STANDARD.

sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown: STATE LAW: the **West Virginia Consumer Credit and Protection Act (WVCCPA), W. Va. Code Ch. 46A** — especially **Article 6 (General Consumer Protection)** — reaches unfair/deceptive home-repair practices and is enforced by the AG's Consumer Protection Division (with a private right of action). Door-to-door work carries a **3-business-day right to cancel** under **W. Va. Code § 46A-2-132 (home solicitation; buyer's right to cancel)**, with the required cancellation notice at **§ 46A-2-133** — cancellable until midnight of the third business day; notice may be in any written form. Home-improvement transactions have their own rule at **W. Va. C.S.R. § 142-5-3**. Complaints: WV AG Consumer Protection.

sections.rawHeading: 5 · Permits & codes (GOV — medium; State Fire Commission base, local enforcement)
sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.confidenceNote: medium; State Fire Commission base, local enforcement
sections.markdown: STATE LAW/LOCAL: WV adopts the **State Building Code through the State Fire Commission** on an ICC/IRC base (**verify current IRC cycle before publish**), but **enforcement is local** — many rural counties have limited or no building-inspection apparatus, while cities (**Charleston, Huntington, Morgantown, Wheeling, Parkersburg**) run active departments. Chimney relines, rebuilds, and solid-fuel appliance installs are generally permit work where a department exists; in unincorporated rural areas there may be no permit process at all. This state needs the local-variance disclaimer.

sections.rawHeading: 6 · CO law (GOV — high confidence; new construction + rentals, not owner-occupied resales)
sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence; new construction + rentals, not owner-occupied resales
sections.markdown: STATE LAW: **W. Va. Code § 15A-10-12** ("Smoke detectors in one- and two-family dwellings; carbon monoxide detectors" — the State Fire Marshal article; the former fire-code section in Ch. 29 is now shown as repealed) requires an operational **CO detector in any newly constructed residential unit with a fuel-burning heating or cooking source**, in residential units connected to such a newly constructed building, in **one- and two-family dwellings intended to be rented or leased, hotels, and motels**, and in schools/daycares with fuel-burning devices; detectors plug into an unswitched outlet or are hardwired with battery backup (hardwired required in new construction). *(Smoke-detector coverage details not re-read Sep 2026.)* Coverage is triggered by **new construction and rental**, not by resale of an existing owner-occupied home — **no statewide pre-sale CO certificate.** Violation is a misdemeanor with graduated fines: **$250 first offense, $750 second, $2,000 third and subsequent**. A permitted chimney job is the natural moment to add alarms.

sections.title: Solid fuel and environmental rules
sections.markdown: No statewide burn-ban or stove-emission regime. Not a material content section for WV.

sections.rawHeading: 8 · Scam landscape (REF — partial; pull specifics before publish)
sections.title: Scam patterns and enforcement
sections.markdown: The WV AG's Consumer Protection Division pursues home-repair contractors, and the door-knock "we noticed your chimney" pitch is a textbook § 46A-2-132 home-solicitation + WVCCPA violation; unlicensed $5,000+ residential work is separately actionable under the Contractor Licensing Act (ch. 30, art. 42). **Specific WV chimney-sweep enforcement actions: NOT YET CONFIRMED — re-run search before publish.**

story.heading: The story
story.markdown: West Virginia **CONFIRMS the master finding, and does so almost to the letter.** It is one of the few states with a **real statewide contractor license that reaches chimney repair** ($5,000 residential threshold under ch. 30, art. 42 — recodified and raised; re-verified Sep 2026) — a strong-license regime — and, exactly as the correlation predicts, its **sale side is hollow: caveat emptor, with no statutory seller-disclosure article located in the current Code.** Strong on the credential, hollow on the sale. The notable operational quirk is the **sweep-vs-repair split at $5,000**: a sweep-only visit (and now most mid-size repairs) can be unlicensed while big repointing needs a licensed contractor — a clean line the page can teach consumers to watch for. Batch-2 addendum: despite the real license, **"insured" is meaningless at state level** — no liability minimum attaches to it, and the only bond (wage bond, § 21-5-14 — batch-2 cite, not re-read Sep 2026) protects employees, not homeowners.
